content.goal: Give ATLAS a session that remembers the conversation across turns.
content.why: The model is stateless — memory is an illusion YOU create by re-sending history. A small session object holds it outside the model. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 2 and Ch 9.)
content.verify: The file saves. The session's messages list IS the conversation — the entire memory, carried on every call.

content.goal: Have a two-turn conversation that proves memory works.
content.why: A follow-up like "what did I just ask?" only works if you resend the earlier turns. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 2, section 2.2.)
content.code:
session.user("My favorite language is Java.")
reply = ask(session.messages); session.assistant(reply); print(reply)

session.user("What is my favorite language?")
reply = ask(session.messages); session.assistant(reply); print(reply)
content.verify: The second answer correctly says "Java" — because you resent the whole history. Remove the first two lines and it can no longer know; that proves the memory lives in the messages you send, not in the model.

content.goal: Add truncation (a sliding window) to keep the conversation from overflowing.
content.why: Long conversations overflow the finite context "desk" and cost more each turn. Truncation is the simplest fix — keep the system prompt plus the most recent messages. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 9, section 9.3.)
content.code:
def trimmed(messages, keep_recent=6):
    system = messages[0:1]              # always keep the system prompt
    recent = messages[1:][-keep_recent:]  # keep only the last N turns
    return system + recent
# Use ask(trimmed(session.messages)) for very long chats.
content.verify: On a long conversation, only the system prompt plus the last few turns are sent. Confirm by printing len(trimmed(session.messages)) — it stays bounded no matter how long the chat grows.
content.troubleshoot: Truncation risks forgetting an important EARLY fact. If early context matters, prefer summarization (next step) over dropping messages.

content.goal: Add summarization — compress old turns into a short summary instead of dropping them.
content.why: Summarization preserves the gist of early messages while using far fewer tokens — the standard 2026 technique for long-running agents. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 9, section 9.3.)
content.code:
def summarize_old(messages, keep_recent=4):
    system = messages[0]
    old = messages[1:-keep_recent]
    recent = messages[-keep_recent:]
    if len(old) < 2:
        return messages
    summary = ask([
        {"role": "system", "content": "Summarize this conversation so far in 2-3 sentences, keeping key facts."},
        {"role": "user", "content": str(old)},
    ])
    return [system, {"role": "system", "content": f"Summary so far: {summary}"}] + recent
content.verify: After many turns, the old messages collapse into one short "Summary so far:" line, and ATLAS still recalls key facts (like "Java") from the summary rather than the raw transcript.
content.troubleshoot: If the summary drops a detail that later matters, tighten the summarizer prompt ("keep names, preferences, and decisions"). Summarize WITH the goal in mind.

content.goal: Add a tiny profile (key-value) memory that persists across runs.
content.why: Not every memory needs machinery — a small store of facts, loaded into the system prompt each run, covers a lot. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 9, section 9.4.)
content.verify: A profile.json file appears with the stored fact. Start a brand-new run and ATLAS already knows your favorite language — memory that survives ACROSS runs, not just within one.

content.why: You have both within-run working memory and across-run persistent memory — the distinction from Chapter 7 made real.
content.verify: All true — the session carries conversation history; truncation bounds long chats; summarization preserves early facts cheaply; a profile.json persists facts across runs. You understand the universal shape: store outside the model, retrieve the relevant slice, place it on the desk. Next unit adds retrieval by MEANING with embeddings.
